description:
PhD Cost of Living: UK, Germany & Netherlands (2027)

Direct answer box (first 50 words):

A realistic monthly budget for a PhD student in 2026–27 is roughly £1,100–£1,600 in the UK (more in London), €950–€1,400 in Germany, and €1,300–€1,800 in the Netherlands — housing dominating every budget. Whether that's comfortable depends on your funding: stipends in all three countries are tight but workable outside the priciest cities.

The three budgets at a glance

These are single-person, modest-lifestyle estimates for 2026–27. Rents especially vary enormously within each country — treat the city tiers as guides and verify current listings before committing.

Utilities & internet£80–£120£100–£150€80–€130€90–€150€120–€180 (often partly included)€150–€200
Food£200–£280£250–£350€200–€300€250–€350€250–€350€300–€400
Transport£50–£90£100–£160€0–€49 (Deutschlandticket)€0–€49€20–€60 (bike + discount card)€30–€80
Health insuranceIncluded via NHS surcharge/low-income exemptions—€120–€160 (public, student/subsidised rates vary)€130–€180€120–€140 (basic insurance; healthcare allowance may offset)€120–€140

Rough total£1,100–£1,600£1,500–£2,300€950–€1,400€1,300–€1,900€1,300–€1,800€1,600–€2,300

The pattern is consistent: rent decides everything. A stipend that is comfortable in a German or British provincial city can be genuinely tight in London, Amsterdam or Munich. For how your income compares, see our PhD stipend and salary comparison by country.

United Kingdom: stipends vs reality

A typical UK doctoral stipend sits around £19,000–£20,000 per year, tax-free — roughly £1,600/month, slightly higher with the London weighting. That covers a mid-tier city comfortably-ish and London only with flatsharing and discipline.

What moves UK budgets:

  • Visa-related costs before you arrive: the visa fee and the Immigration Health Surcharge are significant one-off payments — our UK student visa financial requirements guide lists the exact amounts you must show and pay.
  • Accommodation type. University halls are convenient but rarely the cheapest for doctoral students; shared private flats usually win — compare options before signing anything.
  • One-off setup costs. Deposit (usually 5 weeks' rent), guarantee requirements for international students without UK credit history, and winter energy bills.

Budget honestly for the first two months: setup costs routinely add £1,000–£1,500 before routine spending settles.

Germany: still the cheapest of the three

Germany's combination of no tuition, subsidised student services and moderate rents keeps it the most affordable — with clear exceptions:

City tierExamplesRealistic monthly total
Affordable university citiesLeipzig, Dresden, Magdeburg, Kaiserslautern€900–€1,200
Mid-tierBerlin (rising), Göttingen, Tübingen, Aachen, Darmstadt€1,100–€1,400
ExpensiveMunich, Hamburg, Frankfurt, Stuttgart€1,400–€1,900

Points that surprise newcomers:

  • Deutschlandticket (currently around €49–€58/month, price subject to change) gives nationwide regional transport — a genuinely large saving in most cities.
  • Semester contribution at universities (€100–€400/semester) often includes a regional transport ticket.
  • Mandatory health insurance costs students roughly €120–€160/month; once your PhD is an employment contract, the employer shares the cost — a hidden advantage of E13 positions, as explained in our TV-L E13 salary guide.
  • Visa proof of funds: if you need a blocked account for your German visa, the required amount (~€11,904/year for the current student rate — verify) is calibrated to roughly this budget. Details in our blocked account guide.

Netherlands: highest costs, best salary floor

Dutch living costs run between the UK and Germany — but the housing market is the hardest in Europe for newcomers. The salary floor is the compensating factor: every PhD candidate earns the fixed employee scale (~€2,901→~€3,707 gross across four years), as set out in our PhD in the Netherlands salary and contract guide.

Realistic monthly budgets:

City tierExamplesRealistic monthly total
More affordable student citiesGroningen, Nijmegen, Wageningen, Twente/Enschede, Tilburg€1,200–€1,500
Mid-tierDelft, Eindhoven, Leiden, Rotterdam€1,400–€1,800
Tightest marketsAmsterdam, Utrecht€1,700–€2,300
  • Basic health insurance is mandatory (~€120–€140/month); many PhD employees qualify for the zorgtoeslag healthcare allowance, which offsets a chunk of it — check on toeslagen.nl.
  • Bikes are the transport budget: €20–€80/month covers most candidates' transport needs.
  • Housing strategy: university short-stay housing (often first-year only), then a competitive private market. Begin searching before you arrive; "huisjesmelker" scams target internationals — never pay deposits before verifying.

How to budget against your actual funding

Match your expected monthly income to the city's total above:

Funding typeApprox. monthly incomeVerdict
UK stipend~£1,600 (more in London)Fine outside London; tight in London
German E13 at 50–75% (net)~€1,700–€2,300Comfortable in most German cities
Dutch PhD salary (net)~€2,200–€2,500 + allowancesComfortable except Amsterdam/Utrecht rents
DAAD-type scholarships~€992–€1,400Tight; Germany's low costs + often subsidised housing make it work — see our DAAD guide

Three rules that survive any city:

  1. Keep a 3-month buffer before you arrive — deposits, setup costs and late first payments are universal.
  2. Fix housing first, everything else second. Rent is 40–60% of every budget above.
  3. Verify all figures at decision time. Prices move; the ranges here are planning estimates for 2026–27.

Hidden costs applicants forget to budget

Beyond the monthly totals, these one-off and recurring costs repeatedly catch new PhD students out:

CostUKGermanyNetherlands
Visa application + health surcharge/ticketVisa fee + Immigration Health Surcharge (often £1,000+ over a PhD's duration — verify)Visa fee ~€75Reduced via university sponsorship; verify with HR
Proof-of-funds mechanicsBank statements/maintenance loan evidenceBlocked account deposit (~€11,904/year) + provider feesUsually none for salaried PhDs (contract is the proof)
Deposit + first rent~5 weeks' rent + first monthUsually 3 months' deposit (Kaution) + first month1–2 months' deposit + first month
Setup (bed, kitchenware, bike)£300–£600€200–€400€200–€400 (plus a bike — budget €100–€300 second-hand)
Semester/admin feesUsually included in tuition€100–€400 per semesterNone for employees

Two practical mitigations:

  • Second-hand first. German and Dutch student cities have active second-hand markets (local marketplace groups, university noticeboards) — most candidates furnish a flat for under €300.
  • Check student discounts even as a PhD employee. Germany's Deutschlandticket and various cultural discounts apply broadly; Dutch universities extend sports and facility access to employees. Ask HR what your staff card covers — it's often more than you expect.

If funding is the bottleneck rather than costs, remember the funding model differs by country: salaried contracts in Germany and the Netherlands versus competitive studentships and scholarships in the UK — our funding comparison and the fully funded scholarships listing are the practical starting points.

Frequently asked questions

Which country is cheapest for a PhD student: UK, Germany or the Netherlands? Germany is generally cheapest overall — no tuition, moderate rents and cheap transport. The UK is more expensive, especially London; the Netherlands sits in between, with the worst housing market of the three.

Can I live on a PhD stipend in London? Yes, but only with shared accommodation and careful budgeting — a standard stipend roughly matches London's modest costs with little margin. A London-weighted stipend or additional funding makes it workable; check what your funder actually pays.

How much should I save before starting a PhD abroad? Plan on a three-month buffer plus setup costs: roughly £3,000–£4,000 for the UK, €2,500–€4,000 for Germany, and €3,000–€4,500 for the Netherlands. Visa routes also require proof of funds — a German blocked account or UK financial maintenance evidence.

Do PhD salaries in Germany and the Netherlands cover health insurance? Yes. In Germany, an employment contract splits the public insurance cost with your employer; in the Netherlands, you pay basic insurance yourself (~€120–€140/month) but may receive a government healthcare allowance depending on income.

Official source

Prices and funding requirements change constantly. Verify current figures on official sources: UKCISA and gov.uk for UK costs and visa funds, DAAD and Deutsche Studentenwerk for Germany, and UNL/toeslagen.nl for the Netherlands — plus local listings for actual rents.
